forecast.session_note: Pre-event note for 31 Aug–4 Sep 2026. The week's organising fact is that Warsh's 28 Aug Jackson Hole keynote turned the 16-17 Sept FOMC into roughly a coin flip (CNBC/CME FedWatch ~50%, up from the post-July-payrolls trough), with inflation named the Fed's 'predominant focus' and labour-market risk explicitly downplayed. That reaction function matters more than the data itself: it means activity/wage beats convert into rate pricing more efficiently than misses do. USD sits mid-range and technically indecisive — DXY 99.21 sitting exactly on its 200SMA (99.18) with RSI 40.7, EUR/USD 1.1643 just above its 200SMA (1.1629) and mid the 1.1515–1.1699 20d range — i.e. positioning does not look stretched either way ahead of ISM (1 Sep) and payrolls (4 Sep). Euro-area core is a low-beta event because the ECB's 10 Sept hike is close to fully discounted (Reuters, 26 Aug: policymakers ready to move, little appetite to signal more), and today's German flash (HICP 2.9% vs 3.1% expected, core steady at 2.4%) removes much of the upside tail. Bailey speaks with only ~15% priced for 17 Sept, so the sterling asymmetry sits on the hawkish side even though a structural, non-tactical speech is the base case. Two leans carry real evidential weight (ISM above, EUR core in line); payrolls genuinely does not separate from consensus and is marked as such.

forecasts.event: US ISM Manufacturing PMI, August 2026 (ISM, 10:00 ET / 14:00 GMT, 1 Sep)

evidence.fact: NY Fed Empire State (17 Aug) rose to 20.6 from 15.6 vs ~11 expected, highest in more than four years; new orders 17.3, shipments 11.7, unfilled orders +11pts to 15.5 and delivery times +8pts to 20.6 — lengthening supplier deliveries mechanically add to the ISM headline (15% weight).
Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing Business Outlook for August printed 47.4 vs 25.0 expected, with six-month optimism reported as the strongest since 1983.

Recent track record: July ISM was 55.6 vs 54.0 consensus (PNC: 'exceeded expectations… broad-based improvement'), the third consecutive factory report to run past forecasts; the employment sub-index crossed 50 for the first time in 33 months and production hit 58.5.
S&P Global flash US manufacturing PMI for August fell to 53.2 from 53.9 vs 53.9 expected — weakest since March, held back by higher fuel costs, less inventory building and supply delays.
Chicago Business Barometer collapsed 10.5pts to 47.1 in August, though this series has been an unreliable ISM predictor and is heavily Chicago-district specific.
Base rate: consensus already embeds mild mean reversion (-0.4pt) from a four-year high, which is the normal statistical prior after an outlier month.

forecasts.lean_rationale: The two regional surveys that historically map best onto the ISM (Empire, Philadelphia) were both large upside surprises in August, and Empire's lengthening delivery times and rising unfilled orders feed the ISM headline positively. The offsetting signals — S&P Global flash and Chicago — are real but the S&P series has run persistently below ISM through 2026 (53.9 vs 55.6 in July), so its miss does not translate one-for-one. On balance the evidence leans above 55.2, most likely to the 55–57 zone rather than a large beat.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Two high-weight leading indicators point the same way and the series has beaten three months running, but the flash PMI/Chicago divergence is genuine and ISM month-to-month noise is roughly ±1.5pt.
forecasts.whats_priced: With the September FOMC near a coin flip, the market is already carrying a 'strong real activity, sticky inflation' narrative — Warsh said he was 'impressed' by the economy's strength. Another solid factory print is therefore largely consistent with what is discounted; DXY at 99.21 with RSI 40.7 sitting on the 200SMA suggests the dollar is not positioned long for it. Prices-paid detail is the underpriced part: fuel-driven cost pressure feeds the hawkish story more than the headline does.
forecasts.asymmetry: Skewed. A beat is more likely but partly discounted, so it plausibly produces only a modest, sub-1SD dollar move. A sub-54 print would be the genuine surprise — it would validate the flash PMI/Chicago signal and undercut the activity leg of hike pricing, so the larger move sits on the downside despite lower probability.

reactions.if_outcome: ISM prints at or above ~56 with prices paid elevated
reactions.then_currency: Would likely support the dollar into payrolls, with DXY holding above the 200SMA at 99.18 and EUR/USD pressured back toward the middle of its 1.1515–1.1699 range

reactions.if_outcome: ISM prints below ~54, i.e. a sharp break from the regional-survey run
reactions.then_currency: Would likely weigh on the dollar as September hike odds are trimmed, with EUR/USD more likely to press the upper end of its 20d range and DXY losing its 200SMA
Limited follow-through likely; USD/JPY, already at the top of its 20d range near 159.70 with a ±0.57% 1SD day, is the pair where even a modest surprise shows up most

forecasts.event: Euro area core HICP flash estimate y/y, August 2026 (Eurostat, 11:00 CET / 09:00 GMT, 1 Sep)

evidence.fact: German flash for August (Destatis, 31 Aug): national core ex food and energy steady at 2.4% y/y; headline CPI/HICP 2.9% vs 3.0-3.1% expected and m/m 0.2% vs 0.3% expected, with energy +10.5% doing the work. Germany is the largest single weight in the euro-area aggregate.
Spain (INE flash, August): HICP up six tenths to 4.5% y/y and core inflation 3.2%, up from 3.0% in July — a genuine underlying acceleration, though Spain is roughly a tenth of the euro-area basket.
France flash: HICP accelerating to about 2.7% y/y from 2.4% on energy, with underlying pressure described as relatively contained.
Italy's core measure was soft into August (core ex energy easing to 1.8% from 1.9% in July data), limiting aggregate upside.

Pass-through channel: euro-area non-energy industrial goods inflation drifted up to 0.9% in July from 0.7%, and services were 3.3%, so the energy shock is starting to touch core categories (August air fares/package holidays are the usual vector).

forecasts.lean_rationale: The national flashes already published point to stability rather than a break: Germany's core is unchanged at 2.4% and its headline undershot, which offsets a firmer Spanish core. Italy's soft core caps the aggregate. That combination is most consistent with 2.5% again, and the residual risk is modestly skewed to a 2.6% rounding rather than 2.4%.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Most of the aggregate is already observable from German, Spanish and French flashes; the uncertainty is confined to rounding and to volatile August services components.
forecasts.whats_priced: An ECB hike on 10 September is close to fully discounted — Reuters reported (26 Aug) policymakers are ready to move but have little appetite to signal more, and the July minutes said the pause should not be read as the end of the cycle. So an in-line core changes nothing for the front end; EUR direction this week is a US-data story, with EUR/USD at 1.1643 sitting barely above its 200SMA at 1.1629 after slipping toward two-week lows.
forecasts.asymmetry: Lopsided toward the upside. A 2.4% print would not credibly remove a hike that is already priced, so the euro downside is small. A 2.6-2.7% core, especially with services above 3.3%, would start pricing a follow-up move beyond September and is the outcome with the most unpriced content.

reactions.if_outcome: Core 2.6% or higher with services firming
reactions.then_currency: Would likely support the euro, with EUR/USD more likely to hold above the 200SMA at 1.1629 and probe the 1.1699 top of the 20d range
Little independent EUR impact likely; EUR/USD probably stays hostage to ISM and payrolls within the 1.1515–1.1699 range
Would likely weigh modestly on the euro, but with the September hike near-fully priced the downside is probably contained near the 1.1629 200SMA rather than trending

forecasts.event: US non-farm payrolls, August 2026 (BLS Employment Situation, 08:30 ET / 12:30 GMT, 4 Sep)

evidence.fact: Initial claims covering the August survey week were exceptionally low: 206K for the week ended 15 Aug (vs 210K expected) and 203K for 22 Aug (vs 208K), with a four-week average near 205K and continuing claims falling 18K to 1.778M — no sign of a layoff impulse.
S&P Global flash composite output hit 56.0 in August, a 52-month high, with services 56.8 vs 54.0 expected — the sector that dominates payroll gains was accelerating.

ADP's weekly NER Pulse (25 Aug) showed an average of 11,750 private jobs per week for the four weeks to 8 Aug — about 47K monthly private — with hiring up a second week. Netted against continued federal workforce slimming, that is consistent with a total near or slightly below +58K.

Momentum and revision record are poor: May cut to +63K, June to +20K, July -23K (vs +85K expected), leaving a 12-month average of about +34K; the establishment survey has been revised down three months running.
Labour supply is shrinking (labour force -264K in July, participation 61.4%, the lowest since early 2021), which lowers the payroll breakeven but also caps the plausible upside to hiring.

The 28 Aug preliminary benchmark revision was only -79K (-0.1%) for the year to March 2026, far smaller than last year's -911K, arguing the establishment survey is not materially overstating the current trend.
Published forecasts straddle consensus: Capital Economics looks for about +90K in August, while FXStreet notes the street is clustered nearer +50K.

forecasts.lean_rationale: The evidence is genuinely split: claims near 60-year lows and a 52-month-high composite PMI argue for a rebound from July's -23K, but ADP's weekly pulse implies only ~47K private before federal job losses, and three consecutive downward revisions plus a 34K 12-month average argue the low-58K bar is not obviously beatable. Recent dispersion is also enormous — July missed by 108K — which swamps any small edge in the leading indicators. ADP's monthly report on 2 Sep is the checkpoint that could shift this.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Signals conflict in direction and the series' recent surprise dispersion (±100K) is far larger than any inference the leading data supports.
forecasts.whats_priced: A September hike is roughly a coin flip after Warsh, having been near-certain after the 9-3 July vote and then cut by the weak July jobs print. FXStreet's read is that a strong payroll with steady wages pushes EUR/USD below 1.16. Crucially, Warsh explicitly downplayed labour-market risk and called inflation the predominant focus, so the market is already inclined to discount a soft payroll number as less policy-relevant than a strong one.
forecasts.asymmetry: Skewed toward the upside for the dollar. A firm report (say +100K with 0.3-0.4% earnings) removes the last obstacle to a September hike and can take pricing from ~50% toward ~90%; a weak or negative print runs into a chair who has said he will not be diverted by labour softness, so the dovish repricing is likely to be shallower than the symmetric-probability view implies. USD/JPY, at 159.68 near its 20d high with a ±0.57% 1SD day, is the highest-beta expression.

reactions.if_outcome: Payrolls well above consensus (roughly +100K or more) with no offsetting revisions
reactions.then_currency: Would likely support the dollar broadly, with EUR/USD pressured through its 200SMA at 1.1629 toward the lower half of the 1.1515–1.1699 range and USD/JPY likely testing the 159.70 range top

reactions.if_outcome: Payrolls in line (roughly +40K to +75K) with unemployment at 4.1%
reactions.then_currency: Probably a limited net move; the September hike stays a coin flip and DXY likely keeps oscillating around its 200SMA at 99.18

reactions.if_outcome: Another negative or near-zero print with downward revisions to June/July
reactions.then_currency: Would likely weigh on the dollar, though Warsh's stated framework argues the dovish repricing may be smaller than the mirror image of a beat; GBP/USD, already above its 200SMA at 1.3428, would be the more likely beneficiary alongside EUR

forecasts.event: US average hourly earnings m/m, August 2026 (BLS, 08:30 ET / 12:30 GMT, 4 Sep)

evidence.fact: July was unusually soft: +0.1% m/m (about 0.6% annualised), taking y/y to 3.2%, a five-year low, with Employ America putting 3m/3m annualised wage growth at just 2.5%.

Mean reversion is the dominant statistical prior after a 0.1% print — the series routinely rebounds the following month, and the 12-month trend of about 3.15% y/y is itself consistent with roughly 0.26% per month.

ADP Pay Insights showed annual pay for job-stayers steady at 4.4% and job-changers at 7.0%, the largest since August 2025 — pointing to supply constraints in parts of the labour market rather than broad wage deceleration.
Composition effects cut both ways: July's payroll weakness was concentrated in local-government education and retail, categories whose losses tend to flatter the average wage.

forecasts.lean_rationale: Consensus at 0.3% already embeds the post-0.1% rebound, and both the 12-month trend (~0.26%/month) and ADP pay data are consistent with that. Nothing in the available evidence separates meaningfully from 0.3%; if anything the risk of a 0.2% print is marginally larger than 0.4% given the 2.5% three-month annualised run rate.
forecasts.confidence_reason: AHE lands within a tick of consensus most months, but monthly noise from composition and pay-period timing is of the same order as the surprise being judged.
forecasts.whats_priced: With inflation, not employment, the stated priority for this Fed, the earnings line has higher beta than usual for a payroll sub-component. The market's hawkish case needs the combination of firm hiring and firm wages; the wage side is the part that has been quietly undermining it, with y/y at a five-year low.
forecasts.asymmetry: The bigger move sits with 0.4%: coupled with a decent payroll it would make the September hike hard to argue against, and it is not in the price. A 0.2% print largely confirms the existing soft-wage trend and should do less.

reactions.if_outcome: AHE 0.4% or higher, y/y turning back up
reactions.then_currency: Would likely support the dollar, reinforcing any payroll beat and pressuring EUR/USD back below its 200SMA at 1.1629
Payroll headline likely dominates; limited independent impact

reactions.if_outcome: AHE 0.1-0.2% with y/y easing further below 3.2%
reactions.then_currency: Would likely take some hawkish premium out of the dollar even on a decent headline, with EUR and GBP the more likely beneficiaries

forecasts.event: US unemployment rate, August 2026 (BLS household survey, 08:30 ET / 12:30 GMT, 4 Sep)

evidence.fact: July's fall to 4.1% — a 13-month low — was driven by a shrinking labour force (-264K) rather than strength, with participation at 61.4%, the lowest since February 2021 and 0.7pp lower since January.
Continued labour-force contraction (Staffing Industry Analysts put the decline at about -1.37M since January) mechanically restrains any rise in the jobless rate even with near-zero payroll growth.
Claims data are consistent with no deterioration: initial claims 203-206K through the survey period and continuing claims down to 1.778M.
Hiring breadth is weak (12-month payroll average about +34K) and the household survey is noisy month to month, so a tick either way is easily generated.

forecasts.lean_rationale: Both the demand and supply sides are contracting together, which is precisely the configuration that keeps the measured rate flat. Claims give no signal of a labour-market break, and the collapsing participation rate means even a poor payroll number need not lift the rate. Nothing here separates from 4.1%.
forecasts.confidence_reason: The mechanical labour-supply argument is strong, but household-survey rounding means a 4.0% or 4.2% print is well within normal noise.
forecasts.whats_priced: The market treats the unemployment rate as the Fed's fig leaf: a stable 4.1% is what allows the hawkish camp to argue the labour market is 'roughly in balance' (Oxford Economics' framing). Stability is the assumption embedded in the ~coin-flip September pricing.
forecasts.asymmetry: The larger move is on 4.2% or higher. That would be the one labour-market outcome hard for a hawkish chair to dismiss, and it is not priced. A 4.0% print would be read partly as a participation artefact and should carry less weight.

reactions.if_outcome: Unemployment rate rises to 4.2% or above, especially with a weak payroll headline
reactions.then_currency: Would likely weigh on the dollar as September hike odds are cut, with EUR/USD more likely to press the 1.1699 top of its 20d range
Likely neutral in isolation; payrolls and earnings drive the reaction

reactions.if_outcome: Rate falls to 4.0% on further participation decline
reactions.then_currency: Would likely offer modest dollar support, though the quality of the decline argues against a durable move

forecasts.event: BoE Governor Andrew Bailey keynote, LSE TRIUM Anniversary Conference, London (09:50 BST / 08:50 GMT, 4 Sep)
forecasts.consensus: No numeric consensus. Benchmark is a broad, structural keynote with no fresh near-term policy signal, consistent with Bailey's recent practice. Read 'above consensus' as hawkish relative to that (opening the door to a 17 Sept hike), 'below consensus' as dovish.

evidence.fact: Venue and format: an anniversary conference keynote, not a policy platform. Bailey's recent set-piece speeches have been structural — regulation and growth at Mansion House (14 July), central bank independence (April) — rather than tactical.

Bailey has repeatedly declined to endorse the hawkish minority: after the 30 July 6-3 hold at 3.75% with three votes for 4.0%, BofA described him as 'fairly explicit that nothing suggests' the BoE is edging toward a hike.

Inflation is running above target and rising: CPI 2.9% y/y in July from 2.6%, driven by the 13% Ofgem cap increase, with the BoE projecting a peak near 3.2% in Q4 and a second cap rise due in October — grounds for hawkish caution if he chooses to use them.

Recent Brent softening has pushed markets to defer the first hike from late 2026 into early 2027 (LSEG: 24bp priced by December, 36bp by February 2027), giving him room to sound relaxed without moving the curve much.
Timing: 13 days before the 17 September MPC, so outside purdah — he is free to guide, but has shown no recent inclination to pre-commit.

forecasts.lean_rationale: The base case is a broad keynote that repeats the 'energy shock, watch second-round effects, no signal on timing' formulation, which is what the market already assumes. There is no dated evidence pointing to a deliberate change in his stance ahead of 17 September, and the venue argues against one.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Speech content is unobservable in advance and Bailey's Q&A has produced unintended signals before; the honest answer is that this is not forecastable from available evidence.
forecasts.whats_priced: Very little tightening is priced for 17 September — under 4bp, roughly a 15% probability, with 24bp by December and 36bp by February 2027; a Reuters poll (13-18 Aug) had 56 of 64 economists expecting no change through year-end. Sterling nonetheless sits high in its range — GBP/USD 1.3583 versus a 20d range of 1.3446–1.3656 and comfortably above its 200SMA at 1.3428 — carrying a modest hawkish-risk premium alongside an unresolved fiscal story (10y gilt yields above 5%, autumn Budget arithmetic).
forecasts.asymmetry: Clearly lopsided. Because only ~15% is priced for September, dovish remarks can remove barely 4bp, whereas any hint that he is closer to the three dissenters could reprice the September meeting several-fold — the bigger move is on the hawkish side even though it is the lower-probability outcome. Against that, GBP/USD near the top of its 20d range and the fiscal overhang mean a hawkish pop may find sellers quickly.

reactions.if_outcome: Bailey signals rising concern about second-round effects from the October Ofgem increase, moving closer to the hike dissenters
reactions.then_currency: Would likely support sterling given how little is priced, with GBP/USD more likely to test the 1.3656 top of its 20d range

reactions.if_outcome: A structural keynote with no near-term policy content, as expected
reactions.then_currency: Minimal GBP impact likely; sterling stays driven by the US payroll report later the same day

reactions.if_outcome: Bailey leans dovish, stressing energy-driven inflation and weak demand
reactions.then_currency: Would likely weigh on sterling, though with only ~15% priced for September the downside from rates alone is limited; GBP/EUR crosses are the cleaner expression than GBP/USD on a payrolls day

resolutions.actual: Core PCE +0.2% m/m (about +0.25% unrounded per Employ America), core y/y 3.3%, unchanged from June; headline +0.2% m/m and 3.7% y/y
resolutions.note: Lean was 'in line' and core landed exactly on consensus on both m/m and y/y (CNBC/Yahoo: both readings as expected). The caveat: our brief expected core y/y to ease to about 3.2%; it held at 3.3%, and the headline surprised 0.1pp high on energy. Employ America flagged the m/m strength as concentrated in portfolio management fees, healthcare and airfares.

resolutions.actual: Q2 real GDP unrevised at +1.5% annualised (BEA second estimate, 26 Aug; JEC calculation puts it at +1.48%, -0.02pp versus the advance estimate)
resolutions.note: Lean was 'below consensus' at low confidence; the print matched the 1.5% consensus to the reported decimal, so this scores as in line rather than a miss. Composition went the other way from our reasoning: consumer spending and business investment were revised up.

resolutions.actual: Hawkish keynote. Warsh said inflation's 'underlying trends' had not improved and that summer's better readings 'do not' settle the matter, called price stability 'not self-executing' and inflation the predominant focus, praised real-activity strength and downplayed labour-market risk; September hike odds rose to roughly a coin flip from about a third
resolutions.note: Our lean was 'no clear lean' at low confidence, so by construction this is unscored. Honest read: the neutral-tone benchmark (roughly 69% of BofA-surveyed managers) was wrong-footed and we did not call the hawkish direction. Bond-market reaction was described as muted despite the repricing.

resolutions.actual: -79,000 (-0.1%) for the March 2026 benchmark level, concentrated in retail and several other major sectors
resolutions.note: Lean was 'above consensus', i.e. a materially smaller downward revision than the -911K March 2025 anchor. -79K is an order of magnitude smaller and among the mildest preliminary revisions on record; Bloomberg reported the median economist projection looked for a larger markdown.

resolutions.actual: Bessent unveiled 'Operation Economic Outcast', a sustained sanctions campaign against Iran and its 'enablers', and said on secondary targets that 'no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions'; Iran said it was 'fully prepared'
resolutions.note: Lean was 'no clear lean' at low confidence; no numeric benchmark existed. The event delivered the pre-trailed sanctions escalation rather than a debt-management surprise, and energy prices remain the transmission channel into G4 inflation prints.

resolutions.actual: 89.4 in August versus 90.2-90.3 expected; July revised down to 90.2 from 90.8; Expectations 68.2 from 74.0, Present Situation 121.2 from 114.4
resolutions.note: Lean was 'below consensus' and the index printed 0.8-0.9pt below, a seven-month low, with the miss driven entirely by the Expectations component (labour-market and business-conditions pessimism, elevated mentions of energy prices and geopolitics). Market impact was negligible, as expected for this series.
